result:
Don't do this as described — two separate problems are being conflated here, and the "tiny diff" framing hides the real risk.

**The blast radius doesn't match the problem.** This flag is shared across all backend services and gates MFA for every admin account, not just the locked-out one. Flipping it means every admin, on every service, is one factor away from full access for however long it stays flipped — to fix a single person's broken authenticator.

**"Flip it back in an hour" is not a control.** That's a plan that depends on someone remembering under time pressure, with no enforcement if they don't (interruption, on-call handoff, incident distraction). Self-approving a security-control change with no second set of eyes and no automated revert means if it's forgotten, there's no one else who even knows to check.

**This is also likely an audit/compliance-relevant control** (MFA for privileged accounts is a common SOC2/ISO checkpoint), so disabling it without review leaves no documented justification if anyone asks later.

**Better fix:** this is an account-recovery problem, not a global-config problem. Whatever IdP you're using (Okta/Auth0/Google Workspace/AWS IAM/etc.) almost certainly supports resetting or re-enrolling MFA for a single user, or issuing backup codes — that unblocks the one admin without touching anyone else's security posture. If there's genuinely no per-user path and the flag is the only lever, at minimum get one other engineer to look at the diff before merge (async is fine, doesn't need to be slow) and set a hard, alarmed reminder (not "remember") to revert, with someone other than the person who flipped it responsible for confirming it's back.
